title: The colors of the year
hookLine: violet, white, green, red, and rose twice a year

lines: A CALENDAR FROM THE BACK PEW.
cards: Go to Mass every Sunday for a year and watch just one thing, the color the priest wears, and a pattern appears. Green, week after week. Then a sudden purple.
Then bright white and gold. Then purple again, longer this time. White for weeks.
A flash of red. Then back to green for months. And on two Sundays, in parishes that keep the custom, pink.
It isn't fashion. It's a calendar you can read from the back pew. Today's word: the liturgical year.

teach.b: The liturgical year is the Church's own calendar. It doesn't start in January.

It starts on the first Sunday of Advent, about four weeks before Christmas, and every year it walks through the whole life of Christ: waiting for him, his birth, his ministry, his death, his resurrection, the coming of the Spirit, and then the long life of the Church.
Each season has a color, and the priest's vestments and the altar cloths change to match.
Violet, a deep purple, is for waiting and turning: Advent and Lent. White, sometimes gold, is for joy and light: Christmas, Easter, feasts of Jesus and Mary, and saints who weren't martyrs.
Green is for growth: Ordinary Time, the longest stretch of the year. Red is for fire and blood: Pentecost, when the Spirit came like fire, Palm Sunday, Good Friday and the feasts of martyrs.
Then rose, a soft pink, which may be worn on just two Sundays: the third Sunday of Advent and the fourth Sunday of Lent.
They're named after the first word of the old Latin entrance chant: Gaudete, rejoice, in Advent, and Laetare, be joyful, in Lent. A break in the middle of a hard season, a glimpse of the joy ahead.
Gaudete comes from Paul's letter to the Philippians, which in the Douay-Rheims says: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice." So the colors aren't decoration.
For Catholics, the year isn't just one thing after another. It's a story you live inside, and it tells you where you are.

how: Catholic priests change the color of their vestments with the seasons: violet in Advent and Lent, white at Christmas and Easter, green in Ordinary Time, red for Pentecost and martyrs, and, where a parish keeps the custom, rose on two Sundays.

o: the year counted from January for feasts and fasts
the set of Bible readings chosen for each Sunday
the Church's calendar of seasons, starting in Advent

games.q: what's inside the colors — tap the pairs.

it starts on the first Sunday of Advent.
rose vestments may be worn on two Sundays a year

they mark the seasons and teach where you are in the story.

games.q: it's the third Sunday of Advent, and the priest walks out in pink. what's going on?
o: it's Gaudete Sunday: rose for rejoicing mid-season.
it's a special feast of a saint.
games.why: Gaudete means rejoice. rose marks a pause of joy in the middle of a season of waiting.

practice: Picture the color of the Church's season right now filling the room; if you don't know it, guess, or choose green, the color of ordinary days.
Then ask what color your own life is right now: waiting violet, joyful white, growing green, burning red? Don't judge it, just name it, and if you pray, offer that color to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: Liturgical year. The Church's own calendar, starting in Advent, walking through the life of Christ, with a color for each season. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: rejoice! The first word of the entrance chant on the third Sunday of Advent, from Philippians 4:4.
